items.title: Why two server instances can lose sight of a new task
items.body:
`const tasks = []` is a variable in the server's memory. When you run two instances of the server, there are two separate processes, each with its own `tasks` array. The load balancer sends each request to whichever instance it chooses. If the create goes to instance A, only A's array gets the task. If the next "list" request goes to instance B, B's array does not have it, so the task seems to be missing. The lesson lists this as a limit of an in-memory array: "it does not scale across multiple instances". That is where a shared database comes in.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing replicates the arrays between instances.
- Module variables live in one process; they are not shared across machines.
- A task is only ever in one instance's array, so it cannot appear twice.

excerpts.quote: At first, an in-memory array is enough to learn flow. Then you should understand why it is limited: - data disappears when the server restarts - it does not scale across multiple instances - it makes queries and relationships harder
const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); const tasks = [];

items.title: What the reference BankAccount does on an overdraft
items.body:
Start: `balance = 0`. `deposit(20)` makes it 20. `withdraw(50)` runs `this.balance -= amount`, which is 20 − 50 = **−30**. There is no `if` anywhere in `withdraw`: nothing checks whether there is enough money, or whether the amount is positive. So `getBalance()` returns −30. The reference solution shows the *shape* of the class, but it enforces no business rule. A real account would check before changing the balance, for example by throwing when the amount is larger than the balance.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing throws; there is no check.
- `withdraw` does not ignore large amounts; it subtracts them.
- `-=` is plain subtraction; it does not clamp at zero.

excerpts.quote: deposit(amount) { this.balance += amount; } withdraw(amount) { this.balance -= amount; }

items.title: Why the isValidEmail tests are short and reliable
items.body:
`isValidEmail` is a **pure function**: it only looks at its argument (`email.includes("@") && email.includes(".")`), and it reads or changes nothing outside itself. So the same input always gives the same output, and a test is one line: call it, compare with the expected answer. No setup, no network, no clean-up. The lesson: "The tests are easy to read because the function has one job and no hidden external state. That is another reason pure functions are so valuable." It also lists pure functions first among the easiest high-value tests.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing is mocked; there is no email server involved.
- `strict` assert is the opposite: it does *not* ignore type differences.
- Node's test runner does not retry failing assertions.

excerpts.quote: function isValidEmail(email) { return email.includes("@") && email.includes("."); }

This example uses Node's built-in test runner to check a small pure function. The tests are easy to read because the function has one job and no hidden external state. That is another reason pure functions are so valuable.

items.title: Why removing express.json() breaks task creation
items.body:
An HTTP request body arrives as raw text. `app.use(express.json())` adds middleware that reads JSON bodies and puts the parsed object on `req.body`. The lesson: it "parses JSON request bodies so `req.body` is usable." Without it, nothing parses the body, so `req.body` is not filled in. Then `const { title } = req.body;` cannot get the title. Either way the handler never sees "Ship it", and no task is created from it.

Why the others are wrong:
- The raw string is not stored; the handler never gets it as `title`.
- Express does not parse JSON bodies unless you add this middleware.
- The route is registered by `app.post("/tasks", ...)`, not by `express.json()`.

excerpts.quote: app.use(express.json());
app.post("/tasks", (req, res) => { const { title } = req.body;
`express.json()` parses JSON request bodies so `req.body` is usable.

items.title: Why parseUser returns null for valid JSON without a name
items.body:
`JSON.parse('{"age": 31}')` works and gives `{ age: 31 }`. Then `if (!user.name)` is true, so the code does `throw new Error("User must have a name")`. That throw is *inside* the same `try` block, so it is caught by the same `catch` that handles bad JSON. The `catch` logs the message and returns `null`. So the caller gets `null`, the same value it would get for broken JSON. The lesson: this function handles "two failure modes: invalid JSON and missing required data."

Why the others are wrong:
- A `throw` inside `try` is caught by its own `catch`; it does not escape.
- The `catch` returns `null`, not `undefined`.
- The catch handles every error thrown in the `try`, not only syntax errors.

excerpts.quote: try { const user = JSON.parse(jsonString); if (!user.name) { throw new Error("User must have a name"); } return user; } catch (error) { console.error("Failed to parse user:", error.message); return null; }
This function handles two failure modes: invalid JSON and missing required data.

items.title: Why "after" prints before the posts appear
items.body:
`loadPosts` is an async function. When it is called, it runs until its first `await` (the `fetch`), and at that point it pauses *itself* and immediately hands control back to its caller, returning a promise. The button handler did not `await` that promise, so it simply carries on to the next line and prints "after" at once. Much later, when the response arrives, `loadPosts` continues and renders the posts. The lesson: "`await` pauses only inside the current async function, not the entire program."

Why the others are wrong:
- `await` does not block the whole program, only `loadPosts`.
- Not awaiting a call does not cancel anything; it just does not wait for it.
- `console.log` prints immediately; it does not wait for pending network requests.

excerpts.quote: `async/await` improves readability, but it does not replace the need to understand promise flow. `await` pauses only inside the current async function, not the entire program.
try { const response = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?_limit=3");

items.title: Start here: the JavaScript job-readiness course and its lessons
items.body:
This repo is a docs-first JavaScript course: ten lessons in `docs/lessons/`, each with matching worked answers in `solutions/`. There is no app to run; the code lives in the lessons. This pack draws on four of them.

Read in this order:

- **README.md**: who the course is for and what you should be able to do at the end.
- **docs/course-overview.md**: the whole path at a glance.
- **Lesson 03**: objects, prototypes, classes, modules and error handling.
- **Lesson 05**: async JavaScript, promises, `fetch` and UI loading flows.
- **Lesson 07**: a small Express backend for tasks, and why in-memory data is limited.
- **Lesson 08**: testing, debugging workflow and code-quality habits.
- After trying each lesson's labs, the matching **solutions/lesson-NN-solutions.md**.

Several quizzes take a lesson's example and change one line ("what if this `return` were removed?"). Copy the example into a file, make that change, and run it with Node or in the browser console.

excerpts.quote: This repository is a docs-first JavaScript training course for a learner who already understands basic programming ideas but needs stronger JavaScript skills to become competitive for a junior software engineering role.

The course is designed as a 12-16 week path. It starts with core language fluency, moves into browser and server work, layers in testing and TypeScript, and finishes with a portfolio-quality capstone.

readMore.why: The async lesson used by several quizzes.

items.title: Why wait(ms) wraps setTimeout in a promise
items.body:
`setTimeout` does not return a promise. It returns a timer id, a plain number you can use to cancel the timer. If `wait` just returned that, `wait(1000).then(...)` would fail (numbers have no `.then`), and `await wait(1000)` would continue straight away instead of waiting the delay. So `wait` creates a promise and gives the timer its `resolve` function as the callback: `setTimeout(resolve, ms)`. When the time is up, the timer calls `resolve`, and the promise settles. Now callers can `.then` or `await` it. The lesson calls this "the promise version of a delay".

Why the others are wrong:
- The delay is honoured either way; the problem is only what is returned.
- Nothing runs on another thread; timers are scheduled by the event loop.
- `setTimeout` does not return a promise, so the wrapper is needed, not just for error handling.

excerpts.quote: function wait(ms) { return new Promise(resolve => { setTimeout(resolve, ms); }); } wait(1000).then(() => console.log("One second passed"));
This is the promise version of a delay. Understanding simple custom promises makes other async patterns less mysterious.

items.title: Why an import beats a shared global function
items.body:
With `import { double } from "./math.js"`, the top of `app.js` says exactly what it depends on and where it comes from. Anyone reading the file can see it, and tools can follow it. Inside `math.js`, only what is marked `export` is visible to other files; everything else stays private to that module. A global `double`, by contrast, is a hidden dependency that any script could overwrite. The lesson puts it in one line: "Modules reduce hidden global state and make reuse explicit."

Why the others are wrong:
- The lesson gives no speed reason.
- Globals *are* reachable from other files; that is exactly the risk.
- An import does not copy the function; it refers to the module's export.

excerpts.quote: // math.js export function double(value) { return value * 2; } // app.js import { double } from "./math.js"; console.log(double(4));
Modules reduce hidden global state and make reuse explicit.

items.title: Concept: how each lesson is built and how to use it
items.body:
Every lesson follows the same shape, so you can find things quickly:

- **Goals** and **Prerequisites**: what you will learn and which lessons come first.
- **Concepts**: the ideas in plain words.
- **Worked Example**: one short, realistic piece of code.
- **Explaining The Code**: what each part does and why. This section often names the most common beginner mistake.
- **Exercises**: labs such as "Lab 03C" for you to write yourself.
- **References** and a **Job-Readiness Takeaway**.

The solutions files hold worked answers to the labs. Treat them as one possible answer, not as perfect code: a solution can show the right *shape* while still skipping a rule a real system would need. Reading a solution critically ("what input would break this?") is itself good practice, and some quizzes ask exactly that.

A good loop per lesson: read Concepts, predict what the worked example does, run it, read Explaining The Code, then do the labs before opening the solutions.

excerpts.quote: ## Goals - Write small tests around useful logic. - Understand what to test first as a beginner. - Build a debugging workflow that scales beyond guesswork. - Learn habits that make code review easier.
`Lab 03C`: Write a function that safely parses JSON and returns a default value when parsing fails.

readMore.why: A full lesson in this shape.

items.title: Why a vanished error message is not yet a fix
items.body:
The lesson's debugging workflow ends with two steps: "5. fix one thing at a time" and "6. re-test the original reproduction path". An error message disappearing only tells you the symptom changed. Maybe the bug is fixed; maybe the error is now hidden, swallowed, or happening somewhere else. The only way to know is to repeat the exact steps that showed the bug in step 1 and check that the *expected behaviour* from step 2 now happens.

Why the others are wrong:
- A comment explains a change; it is no substitute for testing it.
- Reverting and trying something else is guesswork, which the lesson says to avoid ("avoid random changes").
- Changing more layers at once breaks "fix one thing at a time".

excerpts.quote: When debugging, avoid random changes. Use a repeatable process: 1. reproduce the bug reliably 2. describe expected behavior in one sentence 3. inspect actual inputs and outputs 4. narrow the failing layer: UI, state, network, server, or data 5. fix one thing at a time 6. re-test the original reproduction path

items.title: What goes wrong when the return before res.status(400) is removed
items.body:
`res.status(400).json(...)` *sends* a response, but sending does not stop the function. The `return` in front of it is what ends the handler. Without it, after sending the 400 the code keeps going: it builds a task with `title.trim()` (an empty string), pushes it into `tasks`, and then calls `res.status(201).json(task)`, a second response to a request that already got one. So a blank task is stored, and the server tries to answer twice (Express reports that headers were already sent). The lesson's order matters: validate, then stop, before storing.

Why the others are wrong:
- Express does not validate titles itself; the handler does.
- The 400 *is* sent; the request does not hang.
- Sending a response does not end the function; only `return` does.

excerpts.quote: if (!title || title.trim() === "") { return res.status(400).json({ error: "Title is required" }); } const task = { id: Date.now(), title: title.trim(), done: false }; tasks.push(task); res.status(201).json(task);
1. parse request 2. validate input 3. apply logic 4. store data 5. return a response

items.title: What safeParse gives up compared with parseUser
items.body:
`safeParse` has `catch { return fallback; }`. The `catch` has no error variable and does nothing with the error: no log, no message. So if the settings file is corrupt, the caller just gets the fallback value, exactly as if the file had really contained that value. There is no trace of the failure anywhere, and the corruption can go unnoticed. The lesson's `parseUser` at least logs `error.message` (`console.error("Failed to parse user:", ...)`), and it also checks that required data is present.

Why the others are wrong:
- An optional catch binding does not log anything; it just has no variable.
- `JSON.parse` handles arrays fine; the default fallback does not affect that.
- `safeParse` never rethrows; it always returns.

excerpts.quote: function safeParse(json, fallback = null) { try { return JSON.parse(json); } catch { return fallback; } }
} catch (error) { console.error("Failed to parse user:", error.message); return null;

items.title: Why loadPosts checks response.ok itself
items.body:
`fetch` only *rejects* (which is what would jump to the `catch`) when the request could not be made at all: no network, DNS failure and so on. If the server answers with 404 or 500, that is still a response, so `fetch` *resolves* normally. Without a check, the code would go on and try to show an error page as posts. So `loadPosts` checks `if (!response.ok)` and throws its own error, and *that* throw lands in the `catch`, which shows "Error: Request failed with status ...". The lesson: "A common beginner mistake is assuming `fetch` throws on every failed HTTP status. It does not."

Why the others are wrong:
- The check does not retry anything.
- `await` throws for neither 4xx nor 5xx; both resolve.
- `response.json()` does not hang on an error status; it just parses whatever body came back.

excerpts.quote: if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Request failed with status ${response.status}`); }

A common beginner mistake is assuming `fetch` throws on every failed HTTP status. It does not. `fetch` only rejects for network-level failures. A `404` or `500` still resolves, so you must check `response.ok`.

items.title: What #status says when the users endpoint returns 503
items.body:
`showUsers` first sets "Loading...". Then, inside its `try`, it does `await loadUsers()`. In `loadUsers`, `fetch` resolves with the 503 response, `response.ok` is false, and it throws `new Error("Status: 503")`. Because `loadUsers` is async, that throw makes its promise **reject**. `await` on a rejected promise throws the same error right there, inside `showUsers`'s `try`. So the `catch` runs and sets the text to `Error: ${error.message}`, which is "Error: Status: 503".

Why the others are wrong:
- `loadUsers` can fail; it throws on a bad status. It needs no try/catch of its own for the caller to see it.
- Callers *do* see rejections from awaited async functions.
- The text is set to "Loading..." first, then replaced by the error; it is never left blank.

excerpts.quote: if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Status: ${response.status}`); }
status.textContent = "Loading..."; try { await loadUsers(); status.textContent = "Loaded users."; } catch (error) { status.textContent = `Error: ${error.message}`;

items.title: Why 1,000 Carts share a single addItem
items.body:
In a class, methods written in the class body (`addItem`, `getTotal`) are put once on `Cart.prototype`. Each object made with `new Cart()` gets its own data from the constructor (`this.items = []`) and a hidden link to that prototype. When you call `cart.addItem(...)`, JavaScript does not find `addItem` on the object itself, follows the link, and finds the one shared function there. So 1,000 carts mean 1,000 `items` arrays but only one `addItem`. The lesson: methods "are shared through the class prototype rather than recreated on every instance", because a class is "syntactic sugar over prototypes".

Why the others are wrong:
- The class body does not re-create methods per instance; only the constructor runs per `new`.
- There is no later "merging" of copies; there was only ever one.
- Methods are not compiled per instance on first use.

excerpts.quote: class Cart { constructor() { this.items = []; } addItem(name, price) { this.items.push({ name, price }); }

The `Cart` class is syntactic sugar over prototypes. Methods like `addItem` and `getTotal` are shared through the class prototype rather than recreated on every instance. You do not have to hand-write the prototype chain often, but you should know classes are not magic.

items.title: Concept: testing and debugging as ways to reduce uncertainty
items.body:
Lesson 08 opens with a useful idea: "Testing is not about proving code is perfect. It is about reducing uncertainty." The cheapest tests with the most value for a beginner usually target pure functions, validation logic, small helpers, and a route's happy path plus its obvious failures.

The same lesson turns debugging into a repeatable process instead of random changes: reproduce, state the expected behaviour, look at real inputs and outputs, narrow down which layer is failing, change one thing, then check again.

Apply the same mindset to the quizzes in this pack. Before you pick an answer, decide what evidence would prove it: which line runs, what value it returns, what the caller sees. If you cannot point to that line, run the example. A lesson's sentence like "this is a common beginner mistake" is a strong hint about what to test first.

excerpts.quote: Testing is not about proving code is perfect. It is about reducing uncertainty.
- pure functions - validation logic - small utility helpers - route behavior for happy path and obvious failures
